TENANT PROTECTIONS FOR SURVIVORS OF DOMESTIC VIOLENCE, SEXUAL ASSAULT, STALKING, HUMAN TRAFFICKING, AND ABUSE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 · Pat Morgan

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes the protections California law gives a residential tenant when the tenant, a household member, or an immediate family member has been the victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, human trafficking, abuse of an elder or dependent adult, or certain violent crimes, as those protections may apply to the residential property at 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814, as between Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee. It states what the Civil Code provides on early termination of a lease (Civil Code § 1946.7), on changing the locks (Civil Code §§ 1941.5 and 1941.6), and on the right to summon police or emergency help (Civil Code § 1946.8); what the Code of Civil Procedure provides on eviction (Code of Civil Procedure §§ 1161.3 and 1174.27); and what one published California appellate decision has said about the eviction defense. It does not determine whether any person connected with 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 qualifies for any of these protections, does not evaluate any documentation, and does not tell either Pat Morgan or Jordan Lee what to do about any specific situation.

WHO THE PROTECTIONS COVER: THE LISTED ACTS, HOUSEHOLD MEMBERS, AND IMMEDIATE FAMILY MEMBERS
Civil Code § 1946.7 permits a tenant to notify the landlord of an intent to terminate the tenancy if the tenant, a household member, or an immediate family member was the victim of an act constituting any of eight listed categories: domestic violence as defined in Family Code § 6211; sexual assault as defined in specified Penal Code sections; stalking as defined in Civil Code § 1708.7; human trafficking as defined in Penal Code § 236.1; abuse of an elder or dependent adult as defined in Welfare and Institutions Code § 15610.07; a crime that caused bodily injury or death; a crime that included the exhibition, drawing, brandishing, or use of a firearm or other deadly weapon or instrument; and a crime that included the use of force or a threat of force against the victim. The statute defines a "household member" as a member of the tenant's family who lives in the same residential unit as the tenant, and an "immediate family member" as the tenant's parent, stepparent, spouse, child, child-in-law, stepchild, or sibling, or any person who lived in the tenant's household at the time of the act and whose relationship with the tenant is substantially similar to that of a family member. Family Code § 6211, which the statute incorporates, defines domestic violence as abuse perpetrated against a spouse or former spouse, a cohabitant or former cohabitant, a person with whom the respondent has or has had a dating or engagement relationship, a person with whom the respondent has had a child (under the stated parentage presumption), a child of a party or a child who is the subject of a parentage action, or any other person related by consanguinity or affinity within the second degree. The lock-change statutes and the eviction statute use their own definitions, described in the later clauses of this document, which cross-reference these § 1946.7 definitions and add the § 1946.7(a)(6)-(8) crime categories.

EARLY TERMINATION OF THE LEASE: THE WRITTEN NOTICE, THE ATTACHED DOCUMENTATION, AND THE 180-DAY WINDOW
A notice to terminate a tenancy under Civil Code § 1946.7 must be in writing, and one of four forms of documentation must be attached to it: a copy of a temporary restraining order, emergency protective order, or protective order issued under the listed Family Code, Penal Code, Code of Civil Procedure, or Welfare and Institutions Code provisions that protects the tenant, household member, or immediate family member; a copy of a written report by a peace officer acting in an official capacity stating that the tenant, household member, or immediate family member has filed a report alleging victimization; documentation from a qualified third party (a health practitioner, domestic violence counselor, sexual assault counselor, human trafficking caseworker, or victim of violent crime advocate) in substantially the form set out in the statute, indicating that the person is seeking assistance for physical or mental injuries or abuse; or any other form of documentation that reasonably verifies that the crime or act occurred. Where the tenant relies on an act against an immediate family member who did not live in the tenant's household and the act did not occur within the dwelling unit or within 1,000 feet of it, the tenant must also attach a written statement that the immediate family member was a victim, that the tenant intends to relocate as a result, and that the relocation is to increase the safety, physical, emotional, or psychological well-being, or financial security of the tenant or the family member. The notice must be given within 180 days of the date the order was issued, within 180 days of the date the peace officer's report was made, within 180 days of the date the act or crime occurred, or within the notice period described in Civil Code § 1946.

EFFECT OF THE TERMINATION: RENT LIMITED TO 14 DAYS, NO FORFEITURE OF THE DEPOSIT, AND OTHER TENANTS' OBLIGATIONS
When a tenant gives notice under Civil Code § 1946.7, the tenant is responsible for rent for no more than 14 calendar days after the notice is given, or for any shorter period provided by Civil Code § 1946 or by the lease or rental agreement, and is then released without penalty from any further rent or other payment obligation under the lease; if the premises are relet before the end of that period, the rent owed is prorated. The landlord may not, because of the termination, require the tenant to forfeit any security deposit or advance rent, and a tenant who terminates under the statute is not considered for any purpose to have breached the lease by reason of the termination; in all other respects the ordinary security deposit law applies. The statute does not relieve other tenants -- those other than the tenant who is, or whose household member or immediate family member is, the victim, together with that tenant's household -- from their own obligations under the lease.

CONFIDENTIALITY OF THE DOCUMENTATION, THE BAR ON REFUSING TO RENT, AND CIVIL REMEDIES UNDER § 1946.7
A landlord may not disclose information a tenant provides under Civil Code § 1946.7 to a third party unless the tenant consents in writing or the disclosure is required by law or court order; the landlord's communication with a qualified third party to verify the contents of that party's documentation is not a disclosure. An owner or owner's agent may not refuse to rent to an otherwise qualified prospective tenant, or refuse to continue renting to an existing tenant, solely because the tenant previously exercised rights under the section or previously terminated a tenancy because of the circumstances it covers. A landlord or landlord's agent who violates the section is liable to the tenant in a civil action for actual damages and for statutory damages of not less than $100 and not more than $5,000 -- except that statutory damages are not available where the tenant's only documentation was the catch-all "any other form of documentation" option in subdivision (b)(4). These remedies are in addition to any other remedy provided by law.

CHANGING THE LOCKS WHEN THE ALLEGED PERPETRATOR IS NOT A TENANT OF THE SAME UNIT (CIV. CODE § 1941.5)
Civil Code § 1941.5, as repealed and re-enacted effective January 1, 2025, applies when a person is alleged to have committed abuse or violence against an "eligible tenant" -- a tenant who is a victim of abuse or violence, or a tenant whose immediate family member or household member is a victim, so long as the tenant is not alleged to have committed the abuse or violence -- and the alleged perpetrator is not a tenant of the same dwelling unit. On the eligible tenant's written request, accompanied by one of the listed forms of documentation, the landlord must change the locks of the tenant's dwelling unit at the landlord's own expense within 24 hours and give the tenant a key. The documentation options parallel those under § 1946.7 -- a protective or restraining order, a peace officer's written report, a qualified-third-party statement in the statutory form, or any other documentation that reasonably verifies the abuse or violence, expressly including a signed statement from the eligible tenant -- and the tenant satisfies the requirement by providing any one of them, of the tenant's choosing. If the landlord does not change the locks within 24 hours, the tenant may change them without the landlord's permission notwithstanding any lease provision to the contrary; the tenant must then change the locks in a workmanlike manner with locks of similar or better quality, notify the landlord within 24 hours, and provide the landlord a key by any reasonable agreed method, and the landlord must reimburse the tenant's lock-change expenses within 21 days. "Locks" means any exterior lock that provides access to the dwelling. "Abuse or violence" takes its meaning from Code of Civil Procedure § 1161.3(a)(1), quoted in a later clause.

CHANGING THE LOCKS WHEN THE RESTRAINED PERSON IS A CO-TENANT OF THE SAME UNIT (CIV. CODE § 1941.6)
Civil Code § 1941.6 addresses the different situation in which the person restrained from contact with a protected tenant under a court order is a tenant of the same dwelling unit. There, the landlord must change the locks at its own expense within 24 hours after the protected tenant makes a written request and gives the landlord a copy of a court order that excludes the restrained person from the dwelling unit, and must give the protected tenant a key. A "court order" for this purpose is one lawfully issued within the last 180 days under Code of Civil Procedure § 527.6, Parts 3, 4, or 5 of Division 10 of the Family Code, Penal Code § 136.2, or Welfare and Institutions Code § 213.5. If the landlord fails to act within 24 hours, the protected tenant may change the locks without permission notwithstanding any lease provision to the contrary, subject to the same workmanlike-quality, 24-hour notice, key-delivery, and 21-day reimbursement rules as under § 1941.5. The statute provides that, notwithstanding the self-help eviction statute (Civil Code § 789.3), a landlord who changes the locks under this section is not liable to the person excluded, and that the excluded person remains liable under the lease, with all other tenants of the unit, for rent as the lease provides.

EVICTION: THE BAR ON TERMINATING A TENANCY BASED ON ABUSE OR VIOLENCE AGAINST THE TENANT (CODE CIV. PROC. § 1161.3)
Code of Civil Procedure § 1161.3 provides that a landlord shall not terminate a tenancy, or fail to renew one, based on an act of abuse or violence against a tenant, the tenant's immediate family member, or the tenant's household member, if the landlord has received documentation evidencing that abuse or violence. "Abuse or violence" means domestic violence as defined in Family Code § 6211, sexual assault as defined in Code of Civil Procedure § 1219, stalking as defined in Civil Code § 1708.7 or Penal Code § 646.9, human trafficking as defined in Penal Code § 236.1, abuse of an elder or dependent adult as defined in Welfare and Institutions Code § 15610.07, or any act described in Civil Code § 1946.7(a)(6)-(8) (the bodily-injury, deadly-weapon, and force-or-threat crime categories). The qualifying documentation is a protective or restraining order issued within the last 180 days, a peace officer's written report written within the last 180 days, a qualified-third-party statement in the statutory form, or any other documentation or evidence that reasonably verifies the abuse or violence. The prohibition has two exceptions: the landlord may terminate or decline to renew, even after receiving documentation, if the perpetrator is a "tenant in residence" of the same dwelling unit (a tenant currently residing in the unit with full physical and legal access to it), or if both the perpetrator's words or actions have threatened the physical safety of other tenants, guests, invitees, or licensees and, after expiration of a three-day notice requiring the tenant not to voluntarily permit or consent to the perpetrator's presence on the premises, the tenant continues to do so. A landlord is not liable to other tenants for any action arising from its compliance with the section, notwithstanding any lease provision to the contrary.

THE UNLAWFUL DETAINER AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSE, PARTIAL EVICTION OF THE PERPETRATOR, AND CONFIDENTIALITY (CODE CIV. PROC. §§ 1161.3(D)-(E), 1174.27)
A defendant in an unlawful detainer action arising from a termination or non-renewal based on an act of abuse or violence may raise the matter as an affirmative defense. Where the perpetrator is not a tenant in residence of the same dwelling unit, the defendant has a complete defense to that cause of action unless both parts of the threat-plus-continued-presence exception apply. Where the perpetrator is a tenant in residence of the same unit, the court proceeds under Code of Civil Procedure § 1174.27. Under that section, the court first determines whether there is documentation evidencing abuse or violence; if there is not, the defense is denied. If there is, and the court does not find the defendant who raised the defense guilty of unlawful detainer on any other ground, that defendant and any other occupant not found guilty are not guilty of unlawful detainer, are not named in any judgment for the landlord, and are not liable to the landlord for any amount related to the action, including holdover damages, court costs, lease termination fees, or attorney's fees. On a showing that another defendant was the perpetrator and is guilty of unlawful detainer, the court must issue a partial eviction removing and barring the perpetrator from the unit without terminating the tenancy, and must order the landlord to change the locks and give the remaining occupants the new key; the court may also permanently bar the perpetrator from the premises and may condition the tenancy on the remaining occupants not inviting the perpetrator to live there, taking into account custody or visitation orders and other factors that may require the perpetrator's temporary reentry. A determination that a person is a perpetrator under this procedure is not a finding of that fact for any other purpose and is not admissible as evidence that the person committed a crime or is a perpetrator in any other proceeding. Separately, § 1161.3(e) bars the landlord from disclosing information a tenant provides under the section to a third party without the tenant's written consent or a legal or court-ordered requirement.

HOW ONE PUBLISHED DECISION READ THE EVICTION DEFENSE: ELMASSIAN V. FLORES (2021)
In Elmassian v. Flores, the Appellate Division of the Los Angeles County Superior Court, in a certified-for-publication opinion it described as a matter of first impression, construed the then-current text of Code of Civil Procedure § 1161.3. A landlord had evicted a tenant for nuisance; the trial court directed a verdict against the tenant's domestic-violence defense, and a jury found a nuisance. The majority reversed, holding first that a tenant can assert the defense against an eviction based on domestic violence causing a nuisance even where non-domestic-violence grounds are also asserted: a tenant can still be evicted on grounds unrelated to domestic violence -- such as nonpayment of rent or a nuisance created for other reasons -- but where the action rests on both kinds of grounds, the tenant must be allowed to maintain the defense as to the domestic-violence grounds. The majority agreed with the landlord that the existence of domestic violence is not a talisman that defeats an eviction regardless of valid grounds. Second, the majority held that the peace-officer-report form of documentation was satisfied by a one-page police investigative report narrating the tenant's own account of a single incident, which did not name the perpetrator or state his relationship to the tenant; the court reasoned that the statute requires only "a written report" by a peace officer, that requiring the perpetrator to be named and the relationship described would add provisions to the statute, and that requiring documentation of every incident the landlord relied on would impose burdens the statute does not contemplate. The presiding judge dissented, reasoning that the three-day notice and complaint were not "based upon" any act of domestic violence and that the statute's plain language requires that the act or acts relied on be documented, so that documenting one isolated incident does not allow a tenant to invoke other undocumented incidents.

RELATED LAW: THE RIGHT TO SUMMON POLICE OR EMERGENCY ASSISTANCE WITHOUT PENALTY (CIV. CODE § 1946.8)
Civil Code § 1946.8 makes void, as contrary to public policy, any provision in a residential rental or lease agreement that prohibits or limits, or threatens to prohibit or limit, a tenant's, resident's, or other person's right to summon law enforcement or emergency assistance as, or on behalf of, a victim of abuse, a victim of crime, or an individual in an emergency, where the person believes the assistance is necessary to prevent or address the abuse, crime, or emergency. A landlord may not impose or threaten to impose "penalties" -- defined as actual or threatened fees, fines, or penalties; actual or threatened termination or non-renewal of the tenancy; or inferior terms, privileges, or conditions of tenancy compared with tenants who have not sought such assistance -- on a tenant or resident who exercises that right, or as a consequence of someone else summoning assistance on the tenant's or resident's behalf. "Victim of abuse" includes victims of domestic violence, elder or dependent adult abuse, human trafficking, sexual assault, and stalking, and "victim of crime" means any victim of a misdemeanor or felony. Any waiver of the section is void. A tenant, resident, or occupant may raise a violation as an affirmative defense in an unlawful detainer action, and there is a rebuttable presumption that the defense is established if the landlord files the unlawful detainer complaint within 30 days of a person summoning assistance and the complaint is based on a notice alleging that the act of summoning assistance was a lease violation or a nuisance; the landlord may rebut the presumption by showing that a reason other than the summoning of assistance was a substantial motivating factor for filing. A violation also entitles an aggrieved person to seek injunctive relief against the offending policies or penalties, but the section does not permit an injunction prohibiting the filing of an unlawful detainer action.

expectedJSON.body: Code of Civil Procedure § 1161.3 provides that a landlord shall not terminate a tenancy, or fail to renew one, based on an act of abuse or violence against a tenant, the tenant's immediate family member, or the tenant's household member, if the landlord has received documentation evidencing that abuse or violence. "Abuse or violence" means domestic violence as defined in Family Code § 6211, sexual assault as defined in Code of Civil Procedure § 1219, stalking as defined in Civil Code § 1708.7 or Penal Code § 646.9, human trafficking as defined in Penal Code § 236.1, abuse of an elder or dependent adult as defined in Welfare and Institutions Code § 15610.07, or any act described in Civil Code § 1946.7(a)(6)-(8) (the bodily-injury, deadly-weapon, and force-or-threat crime categories). The qualifying documentation is a protective or restraining order issued within the last 180 days, a peace officer's written report written within the last 180 days, a qualified-third-party statement in the statutory form, or any other documentation or evidence that reasonably verifies the abuse or violence. The prohibition has two exceptions: the landlord may terminate or decline to renew, even after receiving documentation, if the perpetrator is a "tenant in residence" of the same dwelling unit (a tenant currently residing in the unit with full physical and legal access to it), or if both the perpetrator's words or actions have threatened the physical safety of other tenants, guests, invitees, or licensees and, after expiration of a three-day notice requiring the tenant not to voluntarily permit or consent to the perpetrator's presence on the premises, the tenant continues to do so. A landlord is not liable to other tenants for any action arising from its compliance with the section, notwithstanding any lease provision to the contrary.

expectedJSON.body: A defendant in an unlawful detainer action arising from a termination or non-renewal based on an act of abuse or violence may raise the matter as an affirmative defense. Where the perpetrator is not a tenant in residence of the same dwelling unit, the defendant has a complete defense to that cause of action unless both parts of the threat-plus-continued-presence exception apply. Where the perpetrator is a tenant in residence of the same unit, the court proceeds under Code of Civil Procedure § 1174.27. Under that section, the court first determines whether there is documentation evidencing abuse or violence; if there is not, the defense is denied. If there is, and the court does not find the defendant who raised the defense guilty of unlawful detainer on any other ground, that defendant and any other occupant not found guilty are not guilty of unlawful detainer, are not named in any judgment for the landlord, and are not liable to the landlord for any amount related to the action, including holdover damages, court costs, lease termination fees, or attorney's fees. On a showing that another defendant was the perpetrator and is guilty of unlawful detainer, the court must issue a partial eviction removing and barring the perpetrator from the unit without terminating the tenancy, and must order the landlord to change the locks and give the remaining occupants the new key; the court may also permanently bar the perpetrator from the premises and may condition the tenancy on the remaining occupants not inviting the perpetrator to live there, taking into account custody or visitation orders and other factors that may require the perpetrator's temporary reentry. A determination that a person is a perpetrator under this procedure is not a finding of that fact for any other purpose and is not admissible as evidence that the person committed a crime or is a perpetrator in any other proceeding. Separately, § 1161.3(e) bars the landlord from disclosing information a tenant provides under the section to a third party without the tenant's written consent or a legal or court-ordered requirement.

expectedJSON.body: In Elmassian v. Flores, the Appellate Division of the Los Angeles County Superior Court, in a certified-for-publication opinion it described as a matter of first impression, construed the then-current text of Code of Civil Procedure § 1161.3. A landlord had evicted a tenant for nuisance; the trial court directed a verdict against the tenant's domestic-violence defense, and a jury found a nuisance. The majority reversed, holding first that a tenant can assert the defense against an eviction based on domestic violence causing a nuisance even where non-domestic-violence grounds are also asserted: a tenant can still be evicted on grounds unrelated to domestic violence -- such as nonpayment of rent or a nuisance created for other reasons -- but where the action rests on both kinds of grounds, the tenant must be allowed to maintain the defense as to the domestic-violence grounds. The majority agreed with the landlord that the existence of domestic violence is not a talisman that defeats an eviction regardless of valid grounds. Second, the majority held that the peace-officer-report form of documentation was satisfied by a one-page police investigative report narrating the tenant's own account of a single incident, which did not name the perpetrator or state his relationship to the tenant; the court reasoned that the statute requires only "a written report" by a peace officer, that requiring the perpetrator to be named and the relationship described would add provisions to the statute, and that requiring documentation of every incident the landlord relied on would impose burdens the statute does not contemplate. The presiding judge dissented, reasoning that the three-day notice and complaint were not "based upon" any act of domestic violence and that the statute's plain language requires that the act or acts relied on be documented, so that documenting one isolated incident does not allow a tenant to invoke other undocumented incidents.

The language of the statute and its legislative history indicate that, although a tenant can be evicted for non-domestic violence grounds even when the tenant is a victim of domestic violence, including due to creating a nuisance for reasons other than domestic violence and/or failing to pay rent, in instances where the action is based on both domestic violence and non-domestic violence grounds, a tenant must be allowed to maintain the section 1161.3 defense as to the domestic violence grounds.

expectedJSON.body: Civil Code § 1946.8 makes void, as contrary to public policy, any provision in a residential rental or lease agreement that prohibits or limits, or threatens to prohibit or limit, a tenant's, resident's, or other person's right to summon law enforcement or emergency assistance as, or on behalf of, a victim of abuse, a victim of crime, or an individual in an emergency, where the person believes the assistance is necessary to prevent or address the abuse, crime, or emergency. A landlord may not impose or threaten to impose "penalties" -- defined as actual or threatened fees, fines, or penalties; actual or threatened termination or non-renewal of the tenancy; or inferior terms, privileges, or conditions of tenancy compared with tenants who have not sought such assistance -- on a tenant or resident who exercises that right, or as a consequence of someone else summoning assistance on the tenant's or resident's behalf. "Victim of abuse" includes victims of domestic violence, elder or dependent adult abuse, human trafficking, sexual assault, and stalking, and "victim of crime" means any victim of a misdemeanor or felony. Any waiver of the section is void. A tenant, resident, or occupant may raise a violation as an affirmative defense in an unlawful detainer action, and there is a rebuttable presumption that the defense is established if the landlord files the unlawful detainer complaint within 30 days of a person summoning assistance and the complaint is based on a notice alleging that the act of summoning assistance was a lease violation or a nuisance; the landlord may rebut the presumption by showing that a reason other than the summoning of assistance was a substantial motivating factor for filing. A violation also entitles an aggrieved person to seek injunctive relief against the offending policies or penalties, but the section does not permit an injunction prohibiting the filing of an unlawful detainer action.
